claims.text: The initial MoNbTaVW refractory high-entropy alloy has a BCC matrix without engineered oxide dispersions.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 1–2 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles during powder processing.
Rigorous pre-milling and mixing followed by spark plasma sintering at approximately 1200°C will produce a homogeneous Y2O3 nanoparticle dispersion.
The Y2O3 nanoparticles will remain finely and uniformly dispersed throughout the alloy's BCC matrix.
Finely dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles act as sinks for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Defect capture by Y2O3 nanoparticles promotes vacancy-interstitial recombination.
Defect capture and recombination limit the growth of harmful irradiation-induced defect clusters.
The Y2O3 dispersion will contribute marginally to alloy strength.
The Y2O3 dispersion will not compromise ductility.
At 1–5 dpa and 600–800°C, the modified alloy will exhibit more than a 25% reduction in irradiation-induced defect density relative to the unmodified alloy.
At 1–5 dpa and 600–800°C, the modified alloy will retain higher yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
At 1–5 dpa and 600–800°C, the modified alloy will retain greater ductility than the unmodified alloy.
The unmodified MoNbTaVW alloy will accumulate more irradiation-induced defects than the Y2O3-modified alloy.
Higher defect accumulation in the unmodified alloy will cause a decline in its mechanical properties under irradiation.
The proposed benefit depends on achieving and maintaining a homogeneous nanoparticle dispersion.
Performance at substantially higher doses or temperatures than 1–5 dpa and 600–800°C is uncertain.
